title: LCA of a Binary Search Tree
statement:
You are given a binary search tree (BST) with distinct integer values: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger. You are also given the values `p` and `q` of two nodes that exist in the tree.

The **lowest common ancestor** (LCA) of two nodes is the deepest node that has both of them in its subtree. A node counts as part of its own subtree, so if `p` is an ancestor of `q` the answer is `p`, and if `p = q` the answer is that node.

Print the value of the LCA of the nodes holding `p` and `q`.
input_format:
The first line is the tree in level order, with `null` for a missing child, separated by spaces. Trailing `null` values may be omitted. The first value is the root.
The second line contains the two integers `p` and `q`.
output_format: Print one integer: the value of the lowest common ancestor.
constraints: p and q are values that appear in the tree (they may be equal)
The tree may be completely unbalanced (depth up to the number of nodes)

examples.explanation: Node 6 lies in the left subtree of the root (via 5 and 7) and node 12 lies in the right subtree, so the paths from the root to them split immediately at 10.
Node 6 is the left child of 7, so 7 is an ancestor of 6 and therefore the LCA of 6 and 7.
The tree is a left-leaning chain 4 > 3 > 2 > 1. Node 3 is an ancestor of node 1, so the answer is 3.

hints: For a general binary tree you would have to search both subtrees. What does the BST ordering tell you about where p and q can be relative to the current node?
Start at the root. If both p and q are smaller than the current value, the LCA is in the left subtree; if both are larger, it is in the right subtree.
The first node whose value lies between p and q (inclusive) is the answer. Do it with a loop rather than recursion, because the tree can be as deep as the number of nodes.
